La géothermie fermée (sondes verticales): Closed-loop geothermal (vertical boreholes) suits almost every project: small footprint, applicable everywhere, no dependence on groundwater. Open-loop geothermal is reserved for sites with accessible groundwater and sufficient flow.
La géothermie fermée est applicable sur: Closed-loop geothermal can be used on almost any Belgian plot. Access for the drilling rig (min. 2.5 m wide) is the only practical constraint. WDD carries out a free feasibility study to confirm.
La géothermie fermée ne génère aucune co: Closed-loop geothermal creates no visual constraint. No outdoor unit, no thermal impact on the façade. Your architectural choices remain intact.

La géothermie fermée repose sur des sond: Closed-loop geothermal relies on vertical boreholes installed underground. They capture the heat naturally stored in the ground and transfer it to a heat pump to heat the building in winter and cool it in summer.
La géothermie fonctionne d’autant mieux: Geothermal energy works all the better when it is planned early. When introduced at the design phase, it can be integrated coherently with the architecture, the thermal needs and the site constraints.
La géothermie ouverte s’appuie sur la ci: Open-loop geothermal relies on the actual circulation of groundwater. It therefore requires more than just drilling: it also requires a good reading of the aquifer, the flow rates and the regulatory context.
La géothermie ouverte utilise directemen: Open-loop geothermal uses groundwater directly, whereas closed-loop geothermal operates with a sealed circuit in vertical boreholes.
La géothermie ouverte utilise l’eau sout: Open-loop geothermal uses groundwater as an energy carrier. The water is pumped, passes through the energy system, then is reinjected into the aquifer while preserving its balance.

Groundwater geothermal works with two separate structures: an abstraction well and a reinjection well. Groundwater is pumped from the aquifer — naturally at 10–14 °C — and its thermal energy is extracted through heat exchange before being reinjected into the same aquifer, far enough away to avoid any thermal short-circuit.

The heat pump boosts the captured energy to produce hot water at 35–70 °C depending on the system, with COPs often above 5. The water undergoes no chemical alteration: only thermal energy is taken, preserving the aquifer's hydrogeological balance over the long term.

The geothermal probe is a U-shaped tube inserted into a vertical borehole 80 to 200 m deep. It provides heat transfer with the ground, which holds a stable temperature of around 10–14 °C all year round.

The heat pump boosts this energy to produce hot water at 35–55 °C, supplying the heating (underfloor heating or low-temperature radiators) and domestic hot water. In summer the cycle reverses: the building's heat is dissipated into the ground, providing natural cooling with no significant extra consumption.
